evidence.claim: Prairie, desert and a mountain climb on the road to Alcova
evidence.quote: As you travel, you'll pass pronghorn-grazed prairie, stark desert, and you'll climb the rugged Seminoe Mountains.

evidence.claim: The Seminoe-Alcova Back Country Byway crosses prairie and desert before climbing the Seminoe Mountains in south central Wyoming.
evidence.quote: The 64-mile Seminoe-Alcova Back Country Byway lies in south central Wyoming. As you travel, you'll pass pronghorn-grazed prairie, stark desert, and you'll climb the rugged Seminoe Mountains.

evidence.claim: Its 64 miles combine pavement and gravel between Sinclair and Alcova; Wyoming’s tourism office gives a leisurely driving time of around two hours.
evidence.quote: The Seminoe-Alcova Backcountry Byway is 64 miles long between Sinclair on Interstate 80 and Alcova on Wyoming Highway 220. Driving time is around two hours traveling at a leisurely pace. The byway is a combination of paved and graveled roads

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents the back country byway as a journey through changing landscapes, with three reservoirs and the Seminoe and Pedro mountains among its attractions.
evidence.quote: Although the road is in a remote area, the amazing transformations in the landscape are worth the back-country journey. Attractions along the byway include Alcova and Pathfinder reservoirs, Seminoe Reservoir, the Seminoe and Pedro mountains, and Seminoe State Park.

evidence.claim: An earlier journey here served the mines: in 1871, a freight and passenger line began linking them with the railroad, paralleling part of the present backway.
evidence.quote: A freight and passenger line began operating between the mines and the railroad in 1871, paralleling part of this Backway.

evidence.claim: Later, construction of Seminoe Dam and improvements to the road brought anglers and boaters into the area.
evidence.quote: With the building of Seminoe Dam and the upgrade of the road, anglers and boaters began visiting the area.

evidence.claim: Driving north, begin at Sinclair and follow County Road 351 toward the mountains.
evidence.quote: Begin at the town of Sinclair, Wyo., at the junction of Interstate 80 and Carbon County Road 351, exit 219. The byway follows County Road 351 north into Natrona County and ends at Alcova, Wyo.

evidence.claim: Beyond Seminoe State Park, the road becomes very steep through the Seminoe Mountains to the Miracle Mile.
evidence.quote: the byway segment beginning just north of Seminoe State Park and running through the Seminoe Mountains to the Miracle Mile is very steep

evidence.claim: The byway crosses this stretch of the North Platte River before ending at Alcova.
evidence.quote: You'll cross rugged mountains and the Miracle Mile, a blue-ribbon trout fishery of the North Platte River.

evidence.claim: At the northern end, County Road 407 meets Wyoming Highway 220.
evidence.quote: To begin at the northern end (Alcova, Wyo.): Begin at junction of Wyoming Highway 220 and Kortes Road (Natrona County 407) and drive south.

evidence.claim: Sinclair began as Parco, a company town named for the Producers & Refiners Corporation, which founded both the town and its refinery.
evidence.quote: The town was originally called Parco, after the Producers & Refiners Corporation (or PARCO), which founded the refinery and the company town.

evidence.claim: Built in 1924–1925, the planned community received a Spanish Colonial Revival design from Denver architects Fisher & Fisher.
evidence.quote: The town was built as a planned community in 1924–1925, designed by Denver architects Fisher & Fisher in a Spanish Colonial Revival style.

evidence.claim: Its historic district includes a central plaza, worker housing, a theatre and a community church.
evidence.quote: In addition to the Parco Inn other significant structures include the Sinclair Theatre and Recreation Hall, the school, the library and the Community Church. The central plaza, business district and original worker housing also contribute.

evidence.claim: The refinery just east of town remains in use, while the historic center became the Parco Historic District in 1987.
evidence.quote: The original refinery, located just east of town, remains in use to this day.

evidence.claim: The district’s name preserves Parco, the town’s original identity.
evidence.quote: The Parco Historic District, also known as the Sinclair Historic District, comprises the center of Sinclair, Wyoming, originally known as Parco, surrounding the Parco Inn.

evidence.claim: the historic center became the Parco Historic District in 1987
evidence.quote: The historic center of town was designated the Parco Historic District in 1987.

evidence.claim: The road’s steep climb north of Seminoe State Park carries it through a range that forms part of Seminoe Reservoir’s northern boundary.
evidence.quote: the range forms a part of the northern boundary of the Seminoe Reservoir

evidence.claim: These mountains contain rocks dating back 2.7 billion years, and Bradley Peak is their primary landmark.
evidence.quote: The mountains sit between 6,000 feet (1,800 m) and 8,000 feet (2,400 m) in elevation, and Bradley Peak is the primary landmark. The mountains contain some of the oldest rocks of the Wyoming Craton, some of which date back 2.7 billion years.

evidence.claim: Gold prospecting and iron ore discoveries followed in the late 1800s.
evidence.quote: In the late 1800s, the mountains were prospected for gold. Gold anomalies were identified at Bradley Peak, and iron ore deposits were also located in the late 1800s.

evidence.claim: The name comes from Basil Cimineau Lajeunesse, a French trapper and explorer active in the region during the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The range was named for Basil Cimineau Lajeunesse, a French trapper and explorer who was active in the region during the 19th century.

evidence.claim: Seminoe is an Americanized spelling of Cimineau.
evidence.quote: It is actually an Americanized spelling of "Cimineau".

evidence.claim: The byway is generally passable May to November. The steep section north of Seminoe State Park to the Miracle Mile is not recommended for motor homes or vehicles pulling trailers. There are no services until Alcova.
evidence.quote: The byway is a combination of paved and graveled roads and is generally passable from May to November. That said, the byway segment beginning just north of Seminoe State Park and running through the Seminoe Mountains to the Miracle Mile is very steep, and not recommended for motor homes or vehicles pulling trailers. There are no services along the byway until you reach Alcova

evidence.claim: The Miracle Mile extends five and a half river miles from the base of Kortes Dam downstream to Pathfinder Reservoir.
evidence.quote: the five and a half river miles from the base of Kortes Dam downstream to the Pathfinder Reservoir, the Miracle Mile Area

evidence.claim: The byway crosses this stretch of the North Platte, which the Bureau of Land Management identifies as a blue-ribbon trout fishery.
evidence.quote: You'll cross rugged mountains and the Miracle Mile, a blue-ribbon trout fishery of the North Platte River.

evidence.claim: Upstream, Kortes Dam impounds the river for hydroelectric power; the Bureau of Reclamation constructed the concrete gravity dam between 1946 and 1951.
evidence.quote: The concrete gravity dam was constructed between 1946 and 1951 by the United States Bureau of Reclamation, with a height of 244 feet (74 m), and a length of 440 feet (130 m) at its crest.  It impounds the North Platte River for hydroelectric power.

evidence.claim: Seminoe Dam was proposed as part of the Kendrick Project to regulate the North Platte and improve agriculture near Casper. Water storage began in 1939, followed that August by the project’s entry into operation.
evidence.quote: This dam was first proposed in the 1930s as part of the Bureau of Reclamation's Kendrick Project, which would regulate the flow of the North Platte River in order to improve agriculture in the valleys surrounding Casper, Wyoming.

evidence.claim: Water storage began in 1939, followed that August by the project’s entry into operation.
evidence.quote: Water storage began on April 2, 1939, when the outlet tunnels were closed. The dam's power station was finished and the entire project was declared operational on August 3, 1939.

evidence.claim: The town was renamed after Sinclair Consolidated Oil Corporation acquired PARCO during the Great Depression.
evidence.quote: It was renamed Sinclair after PARCO was acquired during the Great Depression by Sinclair Consolidated Oil Corporation.

evidence.claim: At the base of the mountains, Seminoe State Park provides camping, boating and fishing facilities beside the reservoir.
evidence.quote: Seminoe State Park, located at the base of the mountains, offers facilities for camping, boating, and fishing for walleye and trout.

flags: The cache identifies a Back Country Byway and describes its attractions, but supplies no designation date or formal designation criteria.
BLM calls the local dunes part of the Killpecker Sand Dunes; Wyoming tourism calls them part of the Ferris Dune Field. Dune affiliation omitted pending geological verification.

Dropped the current overview’s miners’ deaths and gold-rush narrative. The tourism cache supports parts of it, but its generalized account of Native Americans provides no named nation or underlying record suitable for the conflict history.
South-to-north order reverses the material strip’s mile numbering and follows the BLM’s explicit Sinclair-to-Alcova direction.
Miracle Mile is shorter than 90 words because the available place-specific evidence supports a concise river-and-dam story.
Seasonal and vehicle advice is from saved tourism guidance, not a live conditions check. The requested checked date records this cache review.
